The Great Photoresist Mishap: A Lesson in Lithography

Welcome back, everyone! It is great to see you all settling into your new teams. Today, we are going to dive into the physical limits of how small we can actually make our nanoscale devices. But before we get into the heavy physics, let’s start with a little thought experiment to reorient ourselves.

Imagine you are working in the university cleanroom. You have just taken your substrate and spin-coated it with a nice, fresh layer of photoresist. But then you look outside, see it is a beautiful sunny day, and decide to take your freshly coated substrate outside in a clear plastic case for a picnic.

Why is this going to entirely ruin your photolithography work?

When you take that photoresist outside, especially on a sunny day, you are exposing it to a massive amount of ambient ultraviolet (UV) light. Remember, the whole point of lithography is to act like a nanoscale sculptor. You start with a massive film—maybe a whole centimeter wide—and you want to chisel it down into a miniaturized, complex pattern that might only be several nanometers wide (imagine trying to carve out a tiny number "6" or "7" on the surface). To do this, we need to selectively expose the photoresist only where we want the pattern to be.

If you take your sample outside, the sun acts like a giant, unmasked exposure tool. It is exactly like the blue sun-paper (cyanotype paper) we played with earlier in the semester. If you leave that paper out in the open before you place your stencil on it, the whole sheet gets exposed. When you finally take your ruined photoresist back into the cleanroom and try to expose it through your carefully designed photomask, nothing will happen. The chemical properties of the entire film have already been altered by the sun! When you wash it in the developer solvent, you will end up with absolutely no pattern at all. You just wasted your whole day.

Oh, and if your clear case doesn’t have a great seal, your sticky photoresist is now also covered in pollen and dust. Not great for nanoscale devices!

Why Cleanrooms Look Like a Sci-Fi Movie

If you ever visit the cleanroom on campus (it is over in Whitmore Hall on the 6th floor—you should go peer through the windows!), you will notice something striking. The people inside are wearing funny-looking "bunny suits" to keep their skin dander and hair off the devices. But you will also notice that the room itself has a very distinct, amber-colored, red-yellowish tint. It looks a bit like a sci-fi movie set.

Why the strange lighting?

Think back to our picnic mishap. Even standard white room lights contain a jumbled mixture of all colors of the visible spectrum, including blue, purple, and yes, a little bit of UV light leaking in. If we are doing photolithography, we want to ensure our photoresist is only exposed when we explicitly want it to be.

If we look at the electromagnetic spectrum, UV light sits just to the left of the visible spectrum, right next to violet and blue light (wavelengths shorter than 400 nm). To do a really thorough job of blocking UV light, we also need to block the visible light that is closest to it—meaning we cut out all the purple, blue, and even some green light. What is left over? Just the longer wavelengths: yellow, orange, and red. That is why the lithography bays in a cleanroom are bathed in that amber glow. It keeps the photoresist safe until it is time to shine our high-powered, targeted UV exposure tools on it.

Marketing vs. Reality: How Small Are Transistors?

It is hard to overstate how essential it is for us to manufacture these tiny chips reliably and cheaply. You might see news articles popping up where a company like Samsung or TSMC announces they are manufacturing "1.4 nanometer" semiconductor chips.

If you have been paying attention in class, that number should sound a little suspicious to you. We have been saying that the width of a standard transistor is around 100 nanometers. A 1.4-nanometer device would only be about a dozen atoms wide! Are my lecture notes just ten years out of date?

Not quite. The term "node size" (like 1.4 nm or 2 nm) used in these press releases is actually just a marketing label. Back in the 1990s, the node size strictly referred to the physical width of the transistor’s gate—the "valve" that controls the flow of electrons, much like the valve on a water faucet. But over time, as companies kept shrinking devices and changing their 3D architectures, the label took on a life of its own. Today, a "1.4 nm chip" does not actually have any single feature that is 1.4 nanometers wide. It is a bit like buying a sports car with a speedometer that goes up to 500 miles per hour; it sounds incredibly impressive, but it doesn’t mean the car actually drives that fast.

That being said, what these companies are doing is still mind-blowing. The actual gate length on these modern chips might be down to about 10 nanometers or slightly less. That is just a few tens of atoms across! But remember, a transistor isn’t just the gate. You also need the source, the drain, and the electrical contacts. When you add all those parts together, the total footprint of a single transistor is still roughly 100 nanometers.

Moore’s Law and the Incredible Shrinking Chip

Scaling these devices down didn’t happen overnight. It took decades of grueling engineering. Back in the 1970s, engineers could fit maybe 1,000 transistors onto a chip the size of your fingernail. Today, we are packing tens of billions of transistors into that exact same area.

This relentless progress is described by Moore’s Law, an empirical observation which states that the number of transistors on a microchip doubles approximately every two years.

Think about the math there. If the number of transistors doubles every two years, the area each transistor takes up must be shrinking by a factor of two. Over the last fifty years, we have gone from a thousand to ten billion—that is adding seven zeros to our transistor count! However, we are rapidly approaching the physical limits of the universe. You can only make a transistor so small before you are literally trying to build out of single atoms. Many experts believe we are finally approaching the end of Moore’s Law, though engineers keep finding clever ways to push the boundary just a little further.

The Diffraction Limit: When Light Refuses to Cooperate

So, what is actually stopping us from making devices arbitrarily small? If we want a smaller pattern, why can’t we just cut a smaller and smaller hole in our photomask?

Intuitively, you might think that light travels in straight lines. If you shine light through a large gap, it travels straight through. If you shine light through a tiny nanometer-scale slit, you might expect a tiny, exactly parallel beam of light to hit the photoresist, creating a crisp, tiny dot.

Unfortunately, light is a wave, and waves do not like being squeezed. When you try to force light through a slit that is close to its own wavelength, the wave bends and spreads out on the other side. Instead of a sharp, focused spot, you get a blurred, spread-out blob of light hitting your photoresist. This spreading of light when passed through a small aperture is called diffraction.

Let’s draw this out to really visualize the difference between our cleanroom dreams and physical reality.

Because of this spreading, there is a hard physical boundary called the diffraction limit. As a rule of thumb, the minimum feature size you can successfully pattern is roughly equal to the wavelength of the light you are using.

Here at Virginia Tech, our educational cleanroom uses UV light with a wavelength of 365 nanometers. With that tool, there is simply no way in heck we can pattern a 10-nanometer gate. 365 is way bigger than 10! To get around this, massive companies like Intel and TSMC use incredibly sophisticated machines that generate Extreme Ultraviolet (EUV) light, which has a wavelength of around 13.5 nanometers. Fun fact: there is only one company in the entire world—a Dutch company called ASML—that knows how to build these EUV machines. They are arguably the most complex machines ever built by humans, and they are at the center of a lot of global geopolitical drama right now!

Coding the Waves: Visualizing Diffraction

To really build an intuition for how diffraction works, we are going to use a little bit of computer code. Don’t worry if you have never programmed before—I had an AI write the script for us! (I’ve also included the full script in the Appendix at the end of these notes if you want to peek under the hood.)

I asked the AI to generate a Python script that simulates a plane wave (like our UV light) propagating from left to right and passing through a slit. The script uses a concept called Huygens’ Principle, which basically says that every point in the slit acts as a new source of circular waves, and the program just adds all those waves up to see the final pattern.

You can download the Python script from https://tinyurl.com/N1014-260914-code. We are going to run this code using Google Colab, which lets you run Python right in your web browser without installing anything.

Once you paste the code in and hit run, scroll down to the bottom. You will see a visual representation of the wave. The cool part is that you can change the slit_width variable in the code.

If you make the slit width very small (like 0.5 times the wavelength), you will see the wave spread out wildly in all directions—massive diffraction. If you make the slit much wider (like 5.0 times the wavelength), the wave mostly travels straight through with only a little bit of blurring at the edges.

For your homework, I want you to play around with this code. Change the slit width, see how the spreading behavior changes, and think about what this means for the engineers at Intel and TSMC who are trying to print the next generation of computer chips. Have fun with it, and I will see you all next time!

Appendix: Python Diffraction Script

Show Python code
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def visualize_diffraction(slit_width=2.0, wavelength=1.0):
    """
    Simulates a plane wave passing through a slit using Huygens' Principle.
    """
    # Create a grid of points
    x = np.linspace(-5, 10, 400)
    y = np.linspace(-5, 5, 400)
    X, Y = np.meshgrid(x, y)
    
    # Wavenumber
    k = 2 * np.pi / wavelength
    
    # Initialize amplitude array
    amplitude = np.zeros_like(X, dtype=complex)
    
    # Left side of the barrier (Incoming Plane Wave)
    plane_wave_region = X < 0
    amplitude[plane_wave_region] = np.exp(1j * k * X[plane_wave_region])
    
    # Right side of the barrier (Diffraction via Huygens' sources)
    diffraction_region = X >= 0
    num_sources = 100
    sources_y = np.linspace(-slit_width/2, slit_width/2, num_sources)
    
    for sy in sources_y:
        # Distance from each point source in the slit to grid points
        R = np.sqrt(X[diffraction_region]**2 + (Y[diffraction_region] - sy)**2)
        # Add cylindrical wave contribution
        amplitude[diffraction_region] += np.exp(1j * k * R) / np.sqrt(R + 1e-5)
        
    # Normalize the diffracted wave for better visualization
    if len(sources_y) > 0:
        amplitude[diffraction_region] /= np.sqrt(num_sources)

    # Plotting the wave amplitude
    plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
    plt.imshow(np.real(amplitude), extent=[-5, 10, -5, 5], cmap='hsv', origin='lower')
    
    # Draw the barrier (black lines)
    plt.axvline(x=0, ymin=0, ymax=(5 - slit_width/2)/10, color='black', linewidth=6)
    plt.axvline(x=0, ymin=(5 + slit_width/2)/10, ymax=1, color='black', linewidth=6)
    
    plt.title(f'Wave Diffraction (Slit Width = {slit_width} $\lambda$)')
    plt.xlabel('Position X')
    plt.ylabel('Position Y')
    plt.show()

# Try slit width 0.5 - 5 x wavelength
visualize_diffraction(slit_width=2.0)
